**International Copper Study Group Environmental and Economic Committee Twenty Seventh Regular Meeting 6 October 2009, 10:45 a.m. – 1.00 p.m. Lisbon, Portugal** 

**ICSG/EEC27/5** 

# **Index of Leading Economic Indicators of World Refined Copper Usage: Project Proposal** 

# **1. Background** 

At the April 2009 ICSG meeting, the secretariat proposed to member country representatives that, given the challenges associated with forecasting world refined copper usage, it could be useful to examine creating an ICSG index of leading economic indicators that could signal future changes in refined copper usage at the world level. Specifically, the secretariat proposed “…examining methodologies currently being utilized by other organizations, indentifying potential statistical components for a copper-specific index, and testing various methods and components for efficacy and robustness.” At that time, the representative from the United States informed the secretariat that the US Geological Survey (USGS) was already producing a copper leading index and recommended that the secretariat examine the USGS indexes in order to avoid duplication of efforts and to better identify what would be appropriate work for ICSG to undertake in this area. 

# **2. Recent Developments** 

Subsequent to the April 2009 Meeting, the secretariat examined the USGS indexes, exchanged information with the USGS staff responsible for producing those indexes, investigated other methodologies, tested a range of statistical variables related to future refined copper usage and, based on preliminary results, constructed a preliminary ICSG Index in order to better understand if this could be an appropriate and feasible area of future work for ICSG. 

The USGS copper leading index is designed to signal changes in the coincident index, which is constructed with U.S. copper production and employment data. The USGS copper index is comprised of six components: 1) average weekly overtime hours, copper rolling, drawing, extruding and alloying; 2) new orders, nonferrous metals; 3) S&P stock price index, building products companies; 4) index of new private housing units authorized by permit; and 6) spread between the U.S. 10-year Treasury Note and the federal funds rate. According to the USGS staff, those six indicators were selected based on their reliability in signalling changes in the coincident index when tested both individually and when combined into a single index. Other variables tested included shipments of household appliances and contracts and orders for plant equipment but the results were not satisfactory. Given the different index targets (U.S. copper production and employment vs. world refined copper usage), it is suggested that the creation of an ICSG Index would not necessarily be a duplication of USGS efforts. 

The secretariat further examined other methodologies used to construct indexes of leading economic indicators, including those produced by the Organisation for Economic

Cooperation and Development (OECD), The Conference Board (U.S. think tank) and the Economic Cycle Research Institute. According to the OECD’s “Composite Leading Indicators: A Tool for Short-Term Analysis”, the three main criteria for selecting index components are as follows: 1 - Economic significance: there should be an economic reason for the relationship between the leading indicator series and the reference series - Cyclical behaviour: cycles should lead those of the reference series, without missing or including extra cycles, with homogenous lead times - Data quality: there should be broad statistical coverage of the series selected; the series should be compiled on a monthly rather than on a quarterly basis, series should be timely and easily acquired; and the series should not contain any breaks or be revised frequently. # **3. Preliminary ICSG Index** The secretariat identified a number of potential component series for examination and tested their correlation with past, current and future monthly ICSG world refined usage data starting in January 1994. Among the indicators tested were world refined copper exports, world copper concentrate exports, the LME refined copper price, the discount price for No.1 copper scrap, refined copper stocks at the exchanges and at the national and world levels, a variety of stock price indexes (including the Morgan Stanley Capital International Composite Index based on the recommendation of USGS), currencies (the US Dollar and Chilean Peso), interest rates, and national and regional industrial and related indicators such as industrial production, construction, new housing permits, durable goods orders and electricity generation/capacity. Based on those tests, five indicator series have thus far produced the best results: U.S. durable goods orders; the OECD Euro area construction index; world refined copper exports; the No.1 copper scrap price discount; and the Dow Jones Industrial Average. # **Correlations Between World Refined Copper Usage and Selected Indicators, Current Month and 12 Months Forward** 1

Correlations were highest with the construction and stock market indicators, followed by world refined copper exports, US durable goods orders and the scrap price discount. The highest average monthly correlation between these indicators and world refined usage was for the 7 month forward period, followed by the 6 month forward 2 period. Monthly data for these indicators were obtained from the US Census Bureau, OECD, American Metal Market and Platts Metals Weekly, Yahoo Finance and ICSG. In order to create the preliminary index, four steps included in The Conference Board metho

dology for updating composite indexes (also used by USGS) were followed: - 1) Month-to-month changes were computed for each component using a symmetric percent change formula for those components not already in percentage form - 2) The month-to-month changes were adjusted using standardization factors that equalize the volatility of each component - 3) The adjusted monthly changes were summed across the components to obtain the growth rate for the current month - 4) With the previous months index level, the growth rate was computed to update the level of the index. Of note, The Conference Board also adjusts the sum of the adjusted contributions based on the trend of its coincident index. Should future work on leading indicators be approved for ICSG, it is recommended that a coincident index should also be created to allow for a similar trend adjustment. While monthly ICSG data on refined usage date back to 1994, the index was calculated with data starting in July 1998 (= 100) due to current data availability. The current results are preliminary and further testing of both of component indicators, methodology and results would be required before disseminating results. A possible addition to the Index could be a survey of market participant sentiment, which could be distributed and the results tallied over a significant period to measure predictive ability. ## **Preliminary ICSG Index Results** 1,700 150

3 Early results do indicate a high level of correlation between the preliminary index and future world refined copper usage, with a correlation of 0.76 for both the five month and six month forward periods. It does not follow that an ICSG Index could accurately indicate every future change in the direction of world refined copper usage, as indicated by the recent upturn in actual usage that was not captured by the preliminary index. However, these early results would seem to indicate that, following further investigation, it is likely that an ICSG Index of Leading Indicators of World Refined Copper Usage, along with individual indexes of refined copper usage at the major user countries and regions, could be developed to serve as a useful tool for the secretariat and for industry and government members. # **4. Action for Member Countries** Delegates are invited to consider the secretariat’s index of leading economic indicators project proposal attached in Annex I. 4 # **Annex I. Proposal on Index of Leading Economic Indicators Project** 1. The secretariat proposes the creation of a new project to build an index of leading economic indicators of world refined copper usage to be added to th

e Environmental and Economic Committee Work Program. 

2. The secretariat proposes that coincident and lagging indexes will also be created as well as indexes for the major refined copper using countries and regions. 

3. The secretariat proposes that the objective of the project will be build on work already completed by the secretariat in order to produce indexes of leading economic indicators that will consistently signal changes in future world and national/regional refined copper usage and that these figures will be disseminated on a monthly basis. 

4. The secretariat proposes that the project should fully examine the most robust indicators of future refined copper usage, regularly test and evaluate the performance of the selected indicators and indexes and to conduct research on potential new indicators. The ICSG indexes should also be tested against other indexes to ensure that their forecast contributions are unique and significant. 

5. The secretariat proposes that among the potential components series to be added could be the results of a survey aimed at copper market participants. 

6. Potential benefits of this project include providing the secretariat, member government representatives and industry a new tool for gauging future world refined copper usage trends. 

7. The secretariat proposes that ICSG member country representatives will be provided with regular updates on the progress of the project.
